first.rationale: Triage logic: I verify the two inherited beliefs that are both most decision-consequential and weakest relative to the stated objective (sustainable long-term QUALIFIED revenue). memory_73 (promotional pricing) is the memory most likely to be invoked by the competitor's entry pricing and is the single largest potential misallocation: its recorded evidence is 'acquisition and revenue lift' with no stated retention, margin, or cohort-quality horizon, and discount-acquired SMB cohorts are exactly where short-run lift and long-run qualified revenue diverge. If the archive shows the original test measured only near-term bookings, pricing is disqualified for this objective rather than merely deprioritized. memory_31 (signup field reduction) is the second pull: it is the oldest record (day 12), it claims a 'durable' lift on a horizon that may not have been observed, and it is the classic funnel-dilution trap — fewer required fields raises raw activation counts while degrading lead qualification, which would make it look like a win on the two metrics that are currently down while eroding the objective. It also risks being conflated with memory_86; verifying it separates 'cut signup friction' from 'shorten onboarding.' I do NOT spend budget on memory_57 (referral) or memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist) because neither addresses the two live regressions, nor on memory_91, which is recent and whose claim is modest and self-limiting. Current intent: simplify_onboarding, resting on memory_86, which directly targets both observed declines (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) via time-to-value rather than by lowering the price or the qualification bar — the mechanism least likely to buy metric movement at the cost of revenue quality. Caveat: memory_86 itself reports completion and adoption, not downstream retained revenue, so I treat it as supported-but-unproven on the objective and hold the conclusion loosely. Guardrails for the standard experiment: track qualified-lead rate, paid conversion, and 60-day retention alongside completion, and pre-commit to killing the variant if completion rises while qualification falls. If verification shows memory_31's lift was measured only at week one, I will explicitly avoid bundling signup-field cuts into the onboarding change. If verification unexpectedly shows memory_73 tracked retained cohort revenue over a real horizon, I will reconsider promotional_pricing as the competitive response.

final.rationale: Verification resolved both pulls decisively and in opposite directions. exp_73 confirms the trap I flagged: promotional pricing buys signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% while 30-day retention falls -12%, and the source record itself carries an explicit do-not-generalize warning. Against a primary objective of SUSTAINABLE long-term qualified revenue, that disqualifies promotional_pricing outright, even though the competitor's entry pricing is the most salient pressure in the situation. The competitive threat is real but it is not an argument for a response the evidence says destroys the cohort before first renewal; matching a discount war is the failure mode this archive was written to prevent. exp_31 came back clean: retention -1% is noise-level, qualified revenue +4% is positive, so the funnel-dilution concern I raised does not materialize — signup simplification genuinely lifts activation without lowering the qualification bar. Crucially, it is confirmed on SMB and explicitly NOT replicated on other segments, so it is a scoped rather than universal finding. Final decision: simplify_onboarding, targeting the two live regressions (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) through time-to-value rather than price. It rests primarily on memory_86, with memory_31 now upgraded from suspect to verified supporting evidence for the adjacent friction-reduction mechanism, and memory_91 as a compatible in-product complement. Remaining uncertainty I am not papering over: memory_86 itself was never verified and reports completion and adoption, not retained revenue, so its link to the objective is inferred, not demonstrated — the same gap that made exp_73 dangerous. I therefore keep it at standard_experiment rather than broad rollout. Guardrails: scope the test to self-serve SMB where the evidence actually holds and do not extend to enterprise, where memory_44's sales-assisted path is the better-supported route; instrument qualified-lead rate, paid conversion, and 60-day retention alongside completion; pre-commit to killing the variant if completion rises while qualification or retention falls. Do not bundle further signup-field cuts on top of onboarding shortening, so the two effects stay separable. If retention degrades the way exp_73's cohort did, that is a stop signal, not a metric to trade away.
